Thought: Careful, honest benchmark paper: 100 OMIM phenotype entries rewritten from exactly the cited papers, gene withheld, one model, six strategies plus add-ons, scored on a fixed per-paragraph fact list from OMIM allelic-variant text in ClinVar. Main findings: reading strategies are within about 2 points of each other (case table -1.9 the only one beyond replicate noise), and hiding full text drops coverage 77.4 -> 31.2 on 46 entries. The statistics are unusually careful (completion as outcome, ITT sensitivity, replicate and judge variation, Holm, sign tests, corrected-analysis appendix), and the limitations are stated frankly. My concerns for ICLR: (1) every measurement (fact splitting, fact presence, audit, missed-fact attribution, variant name matching) is a judgement by the same model family that wrote the drafts, with zero human validation, so the primary endpoint itself is unvalidated; the planted-error test has no negative controls. (2) The headline 'access bounds agreement' result is close to expected (abstracts hold fewer facts than full text) and is shown with one model; the 'strategies are close' result is a null on a single model with mostly abstract-only inputs (81% of papers), so it says little about strategy design in general, and the paper itself shows differences grow with full text (where n is small, 21 entries). (3) The extract-then-write variants are the authors' own implementations, and the ablation shows their deficit depends on implementation effort, which limits what the comparison says about paradigms. (4) The ML contribution is a benchmark/harness for a narrow biomedical task; methodological novelty is small; venue fit for ICLR is moderate. (5) Hidden-full-text experiment has a confound: only the full-text drafts went through repair, and they come from a different run. (6) Contamination: the memory-only control is weak evidence; abstract-only coverage (about 40%) exceeds what abstracts state (only 2% of missed abstract facts are in the abstract, which suggests conveyed abstract-only facts may partly come from memory) and declines with era. Presentation is dense, with many numbers per sentence; template header reads ICLR 2025. Overall: solid, careful empirical work but limited generality and unvalidated measurement; borderline reject at ICLR.
Summary: The paper introduces a controlled benchmark for writing curated genetics knowledge-base entries from cited papers. 100 OMIM phenotype entries (2-12 references each, stratified by creation era) are rewritten by a single model (Claude Opus 5.5) from their header and exactly the papers OMIM curators cited, with the causal gene withheld and only open-access text available (19% of papers in full text). Six strategies are compared under identical guards, claim-level audit and scoring: direct reading, an agentic curator, an evidence graph, a case table, recall-then-verify, and a memory-only control, plus three add-ons (second-hand evidence from citing papers, case reconciliation, and a learned curation guide). The primary endpoint is coverage of fixed fact lists split once from OMIM's allelic-variant paragraphs as deposited in ClinVar; secondary measures cover HPO synopsis terms, variants, causal gene and inheritance. Main findings: the reading strategies are within about 2 points of one another (only the case table, -1.9, exceeds a measured replicate-noise half-width of 1.0); hiding the full text of the same papers lowers coverage from 77.4% to 31.2% on 46 entries; strategy differences appear larger where more full text is available; a matched ablation suggests the extract-then-write deficit depends on extraction effort; the audit catches 60/60 planted single-fact substitutions but checks fidelity to the source rather than correctness; and a memory-only control by creation era serves as a contamination check.
Strengths: Clean experimental design: sources, model, guards, audit and scoring are held fixed so the generation strategy is the only variable, which addresses a real comparability problem in prior work (FlyAOC, WikiCrow, GEN-KnowRD).

The within-paper hidden-full-text experiment (same papers, same 2,120 fixed facts, paired over entries) is a convincing causal test that input access, not strategy, dominates agreement with curators in this setting (+43.9 points, CI +38.5 to +49.3).
Fixed fact lists split once without sight of any draft avoid denominator drift across strategies; the paper reports that the earlier per-draft scoring gave inflated levels but the same ordering.

Unusually careful statistical reporting: completion treated as an outcome, an intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis, replicate and judge variation to calibrate a noise floor, paired bootstrap intervals, sign tests, Holm correction for secondary measures, and an appendix documenting analyses that were corrected (e.g., the earlier -2.1 evidence-graph gap).

Honest framing of the audit's limits: planted-error sensitivity is reported alongside the absence of negative controls; the 'what it cannot see' analysis of second-hand claims against full text is informative.
Matched ablation separating extraction effort from intermediate representation is a useful check against over-interpreting the paradigm comparison.
Built from public resources with per-entry release of drafts, verdicts and scores; costs and token usage are reported, aiding reproducibility.
Contamination is addressed with a creation-era analysis and a separate set of entries created in June-November 2026.
Weaknesses: No human validation of any measurement. Fact splitting, fact presence judgements, claim-level audit verdicts, missed-fact attribution and non-normalising variant matching are all performed by the same model family that wrote the drafts. Self-preference bias (which the paper cites) could affect strategies differently, e.g., strategies whose wording is closer to the judge's style. Even a small curator-annotated subset (a few hundred facts) with agreement statistics would substantially strengthen the primary endpoint.

Single model. The central null result ('reading strategies are close') is established for one frontier model with long context; it is unclear whether it holds for weaker or smaller-context models, where intermediate representations are usually motivated. This limits the generality the benchmark claims to offer.

The headline positive finding is close to expected: abstracts contain far fewer of the variant-level facts curators record than full texts do. The quantification is useful, but the insight is not surprising, and the strategy comparison is dominated by abstract-only inputs (81% of papers; 46 of 92 entries in Figure 4 have no full text), which compresses differences by construction.

The regime where strategies differ (half or more full text) has only 21 entries and is observational, confounded with era and journal, as the authors note; the paper's suggestion that 'differences grow where more full text is readable' rests on this subgroup and the 38-entry ablation.

Strategies are the authors' own implementations, developed on the same entries used for evaluation (no separate development set). The ablation shows that the extract-then-write gap moves by about 2 points with extraction effort, so conclusions about paradigms are tied to implementation choices.

Hidden-full-text confound: the full-text condition comes from the main run and went through the audit's repair round, while the two abstract conditions are new runs without repair. The effect is large enough that this is unlikely to reverse the conclusion, but an unrepaired full-text arm (or repaired abstract arms) would make the comparison clean.

Contamination remains a live concern for the reading strategies: direct-reading coverage on abstract-only papers (about 40%) is far above what the abstracts appear to state (only 2% of missed abstract-only facts were found in the abstract), and it varies with creation era. This suggests that a substantial share of facts 'conveyed' from abstracts may come from model memory, which the memory-only control (15%) does not fully bound, since memory may be more accessible when cued by the abstract.

Planted-error test has no unaltered controls, so the audit's false-positive rate is unknown, and only blunt single-value substitutions were tested; 'flagged all 60' therefore says little about the audit's practical precision.

Reference is narrow: variant-centred ClinVar paragraphs rather than full OMIM entries; drafts make about twice as many statements per paper as the reference has facts, so coverage measures only one slice of entry quality and says nothing about the correctness of extra content.

Venue fit and novelty: the contribution is primarily an evaluation harness for a specific biocuration task, with no new method; for ICLR the generalisable ML lesson (beyond 'give the model the full text') is limited.
Presentation is dense; many paragraphs pack 5-10 numbers with intervals into running text, which makes the main messages hard to extract. The template header reads 'ICLR 2025' while citing 2026 work.
Questions: Can you provide any human validation, even small-scale, of the fact splitting and fact-presence judgements (e.g., a curator or geneticist marking 200-300 facts against drafts), with agreement statistics? Without it, how confident can readers be that the 1-2 point differences between strategies reflect content and not judge preference?

Have you run at least one strategy comparison with a second model (a different family, or a smaller-context model) as the writer, or as the judge on fixed drafts? Does the ordering or closeness of strategies change?

For abstract-only papers, what fraction of facts the drafts conveyed are actually stated in the abstract? If many are not, how do you separate reading from cued recall, and how does this affect the 77.4% vs 31.2% contrast?

In the hidden-full-text experiment, what is the effect of the repair round on coverage in the main run (pre- vs post-repair coverage for the full-text drafts)? Can you report the full-text condition before repair to remove the asymmetry?
What was the audit's flag rate on the 60 paragraphs before alteration (or on matched unaltered paragraphs)? Without this, the 60/60 sensitivity cannot be interpreted as a detector.
Since strategies were developed on the evaluation entries, how many design iterations were made and on which entries? Could tuning have favoured direct reading as the baseline?

How would the benchmark handle papers with supplementary material, where most variant tables live in genetics? Is there a subset where supplements are available to test whether the full-text effect grows further?
Why is replicate noise compared against bootstrap CIs over entries as a separate threshold rather than incorporated into the interval (e.g., by a hierarchical bootstrap over entries and replicates)?
Limitations: The authors list the main limitations candidly (single model family, no human validation, narrow reference, open-access only, given reference list, no development split, uneven stopped replies).

Not fully addressed: the possibility that memory, cued by abstracts, accounts for a share of conveyed facts in the reading strategies; and judge self-preference interacting differently with different strategies.
The generated entries could be mistaken for curated content; the ethics statement appropriately requires labelling them as machine-generated drafts for expert review.
